title: ASKAP Monitoring of the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields
summary: In the past decade, time domain astronomy surveys across the multi-messenger spectrum have developed "alert streams" which circulate observational information in real-time to the wider astronomical community. Despite this being standard practice for optical, gamma-ray and gravitational wave time domain astronomy for several years now, this kind of infrastructure has not yet been deployed at-scale for radio telescopes. We are conducting a long-term monitoring program that targets the Rubin Deep Drilling Fields using the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP). The primary goal of this program is to provide serendipitous radio observations of all objects of interest in these fields, and circulate that information in as close to real-time as possible. In this manuscript we outline the survey plans and status, the infrastructure we have developed to disseminate this information and an initial data release comprising 5 months of ASKAP observations of each field (although only 3 months overlaps with Rubin) conducted on an approximately 10 day cadence with a noise level of $\sim 60\,μ$Jy. As part of this data release, we present updated high-cadence radio light curves to the tidal disruption event AT2018hyz and the supernova SN2024abfo along with the discovery of two new radio variables, a possible tidal disruption event ASKAP J095711.5+051205 and an in-progress extreme scattering event ASKAP J005026.4-422958. The scientific results from this program along with the infrastructure developed to acquire them will lay the foundation for the integration of future radio imaging surveys into the broader multi-messenger alert stream, leading the way for major facilities such as the Schmidt Observatory System and the SKA.

title: Flux Evolution of PSR B0540--69 and the Spectral Energy Distribution of its Pulsar Wind Nebula
summary: The young Crab-like pulsar PSR B0540--69, located in the Large Magellanic Cloud, underwent a spin-down rate transition (SRT) in 2011 December, after which its pulsar wind nebula (PWN) was reported to brighten up to 2018. In this work, we extend the study of its X-ray and $γ$-ray flux evolution through 2026 by combining observations from multiple X-ray instruments with data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope, thereby constructing a flux history of the PSR$+$PWN system spanning more than two decades. We find that the enhanced X-ray luminosity of the PSR$+$PWN system has persisted for more than 14 yr after the SRT, up to early 2026, whereas the pulsed X-ray flux remains unchanged across all epochs. This confirms that the brightening originates from the PWN. In the $γ$-ray band, neither the pulsed nor the non-pulsed flux shows any detectable long-term variation between 2008 and 2025. Together, these results imply that the additional spin-down energy released at the SRT has been continuously injected into the PWN over decades, placing strong constraints on the energy budget and physical mechanism of the transition. Combining the non-pulsed X-ray and $γ$-ray fluxes measured here with previously published radio-to-UV data, we further construct a broadband spectral energy distribution of the PWN, which shows properties markedly different from those of the Crab Nebula.

title: Simulation Study of Reconstruction of Cosmic Ray Extensive Air Shower with Thermal Neutron Detected by ENDA
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in Radiation Detection Technology and Methods
summary: In the investigation of the "knee" region within the cosmic ray energy spectrum, extensive air shower (EAS) reconstruction by using different EAS secondary particles are of paramount importance for energy determination and composition separation and finally measurement of energy spectrum of different cosmic ray composition. The Electron-Neutron Detector Array (ENDA) is designed to detect thermal neutrons generated in the ground by high energy hadrons which constitute the "backbone" of EAS and carry vital information regarding the primary cosmic rays. At present, ENDA-64, consisting of 64 detectors, is employed inside the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). This work simulates the response of ENDA and investigates the lateral distributions of thermal neutrons. A comparison of the NKG and double-exponential functions for describing this distribution using MC simulation data shows that the double-exponential function is more accurate. The mean difference between fitted and measured thermal neutron density is within ~ 6%. Meanwhile, the thermal neutron density at 10 m from the shower axis, $ρ_n$, depends mainly on the sum of all hadrons energy or the number of high-energy hadrons. The relationship between $ρ_n$ and EAS hadron energy or the number of high-energy hadrons can be well fitted by a linear function on a log scale. This work is fundamental for energy determination and composition separation with hybrid detection by using ENDA in the near future.

title: Resistive alignment of a black-hole magnetosphere
summary: Recent numerical simulations have shown that black-hole magnetospheres evolve rapidly toward alignment between the magnetic axis and spin axis but the physical origin of this process has remained unclear. We develop an analytic theory of this alignment within resistive relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Taking the slow-spin Blandford-Znajek monopole solution as the exterior magnetic field, we reduce the induction equation to a relaxation equation for the current-sheet inclination angle. Our analysis shows that alignment results from second-order spin effects in the Blandford-Znajek solution combined with explicit resistive dissipation. We test this prediction using resistive-GRMHD simulations at several spins and resistivities and find a regime in which the measured late-time secular decay agrees quantitatively with the analytic prediction.

title: Extreme mass ratio inspirals from the Hills mechanism, The eccentricity distribution of Hills EMRIs in LISA
summary: Extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are promising sources for future space-based gravitational-wave detectors. We investigate EMRIs produced through the Hills mechanism, in which a stellar-mass black-hole binary (BBH) is tidally separated by a massive black hole (MBH), leaving one component bound to it. We present the first self-consistent modelling of this channel, combining an orbit-averaged Fokker-Planck treatment of the nuclear star cluster (NSC), three-body modelling of the binary-MBH encounter, Monte Carlo evolution of captured black holes (BHs), and fully relativistic EMRI trajectories to follow the evolution from binary supply down to final plunge. We find that Hills EMRIs are substantially more circular than classical EMRIs formed through two-body relaxation. For an MBH of $4 \times 10^6 M_\odot$ and circular, equal-mass BBHs of $20 M_\odot$ with initial separation of $0.1$ AU, EMRI mean eccentricities are approximately $0.097$ at our adopted LISA-band entry threshold and $0.034$ at plunge, compared with $0.478$ and $0.228$, respectively, for classical EMRIs. Of the initial BBHs, approximately $0.4$ per cent become EMRIs, whereas approximately $60$ per cent of captured BHs do. For comparable NSC initial compact-object mass, we find approximately $1.6 \times 10^{-8}$ Hills EMRIs per year per galaxy, approximately $12$ per cent of the classical EMRI yield. The Hills channel contribution to the overall eccentricity distribution depends strongly on the binary mass fraction in NSCs. We discuss implications for identifying EMRI formation channels with LISA and for quasi-periodic eruptions.

title: Flip-Flop Shocks and Tori in Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton Accretion onto Rotating Kerr-Weyl Black Holes and Their Quasi-Periodic Variability
summary: We present GRHD simulations of Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion onto a rotating black hole in Weyl conformal gravity, described by the Kerr-Weyl metric. The equatorial flow is evolved for spins a=0.9M and a=0.5M and several Weyl coefficients, which enter through an effective curvature parameter k, and is compared with Kerr runs sharing the same setup. For the k considered, the horizon, ISCO and test-particle frequencies differ from Kerr by at most ~2%. However, the curvature term grows as kr^2 and acts at the accretion radius R_acc. The flow is controlled by one quantity, eta=|k|R_acc^3/M, the ratio of curvature-induced to Newtonian acceleration at R_acc. For eta<~0.03 a stable shock cone forms, indistinguishable from Kerr. For eta~0.2-0.3 the anti-de Sitter-like term traps shocked gas behind the black hole and drives persistent flip-flop oscillations. For eta>~1.6 the cone is destroyed and an oscillating torus forms. Spin modifies only the inner few gravitational radii and does not change the regime. In strongly deviating models the mean accretion rate is 1.7-3 times the Kerr value and varies by 20-60% rms, versus 0.1-1% in Kerr-like flows. The power spectra show global QPOs with fundamentals at 2.9-4.8 Hz for a 10 Msun black hole, with harmonic ladders whose 3:2 and 2:1 ratios come from one non-sinusoidal oscillation, not resonances. These lie in the low-frequency QPO band and are unrelated to test-particle frequencies (~70-200 Hz). They scale as f_0=xi f_K(R_acc), with xi~0.7-1.1 for stable cones and xi~0.23-0.38 for flip-flop and torus regimes. Strong oscillations would be detectable within seconds for a bright Galactic source. The required |k| exceeds galactic-rotation-curve values by 18-36 orders of magnitude, so a detected shock-driven QPO would measure a local deviation from Kerr, and its absence would constrain |k|.

title: TeV Gamma-Ray Emission in the DA 495 Region from HAWC Observations of J1952+2924, J1954+2837, and J1958+2848
summary: Previous observations of the DA 495 region, which contains the pulsar wind nebula (PWN) DA 495 and other very-high-energy (VHE; $>100~\textrm{GeV}$) gamma-ray emitters, showed inconsistent results across different VHE experiments, including differences in the measured flux of DA 495 and in the number of reported sources. Our new dedicated analysis using 3071 days of HAWC data resolves these discrepancies. We identify three extended sources, HAWC J1952+2924 (DA 495), HAWC J1954+2837, and HAWC J1958+2848, all with curved spectra, and find a hint of a fourth source. For DA 495, a multi-wavelength analysis, including our results, radio, X-ray, and other gamma-ray data, reveals that its extended emission is best described by leptonic interactions with an inferred magnetic field of $B\sim10~μ\textrm{G}$ and that hadronic components are not required. On the other hand, we interpret the other two sources, which have no confirmed counterparts, as TeV halos associated with nearby pulsars, PSR J1954+2836 and PSR J1958+2846, respectively. These results reinforce the interpretation of DA 495 as a leptonic-dominated PWN and add two candidates to the growing population of TeV halos.

title: Perpendicular transport in isotropic magnetic turbulence. The role of stochastic drifts
summary: In cosmic ray propagation through turbulent magnetic fields, transport perpendicular to the mean field plays an important role in various astrophysical environments. Numerical simulations have shown that parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients exhibit different energy scalings, causing their ratio to increase with energy, but a comprehensive theoretical explanation remains elusive. Here, we investigate perpendicular diffusion using test particle simulations in synthetic isotropic turbulence spanning 6-7 orders of magnitude in wavenumber, together with a theoretical extension of nonlinear guiding center theory that incorporates stochastic drifts. Our approach combines field line random walk and random guiding center drifts to describe perpendicular transport. We find that parallel and perpendicular diffusion coefficients exhibit the same energy scaling only for $r_L \lesssim 10^{-2} L_c$, where $r_L$ is the particle Larmor radius and $L_c$ is the turbulence coherence length. At higher energies, perpendicular diffusion develops a stronger energy dependence, consistently across different turbulence levels. Our theoretical model suggests that this behavior arises from stochastic drifts induced by turbulent magnetic field components parallel to the mean field.

title: Adiabatic evolution of hadronic neutron stars
summary: In this paper we compute several structural properties of static and rotating neutron stars, considering both rigid and differential rotation. To this end, we use a finite-temperature beta-stable equation of state (EOS) extending the zero-temperature hadronic EOS derived by Fortin et al. (2017). We account for the formation of hyperons and the presence of a neutrino-trapped component. Our goal is to provide insights into the long-term evolution of a protoneutron star (PNS) formed after a core-collapse supernova (CCSN) or a remnant resulting from a binary neutron star merger (BNSM). The EOS is derived using a relativistic mean-field quantum many-body theory within the Hartree approximation. Coupling constants are determined using experimental data on hypernuclei and hypernuclear matter to better account for uncertainties in hyperon single-particle potentials. Our EOS models reproduce the typical features of cold neutron stars and PNSs for nucleonic and hyperonic compositions. In particular, they are consistent with measured masses (2.01 M_sun and 2.14 M_sun for PSR J0348+0432 and PSR J0740+6620) and dimensionless tidal deformabilities from GW170817. Thermal contributions act differently depending on composition and rotation state. Finally, our evolutionary scheme provides a simple way to interpret the long-term evolution of BNSM remnants or PNSs from CCSNe, complementing dynamical simulations unable to cover full evolutionary timescales.

title: Quantifying the coincidence between gravitational waves and fast radio bursts from neutron star-black hole mergers
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are mysterious astrophysical transients whose origin and mechanism remain unclear. Compact object mergers may be a promising channel to produce some FRBs. Neutron star--black hole (NSBH) mergers could produce FRBs through mechanisms involving neutron star tidal disruption or magnetospheric disturbances. This could present an opportunity for multimessenger gravitational-wave observations, providing new insight into the nature of FRBs and nuclear matter. However, some of the gravitational-wave signals may be marginal detections with signal-to-noise ratios <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula> or have large sky location and distance uncertainties, making it less straightforward to confidently associate an FRB with the gravitational-wave signal. One must therefore take care to avoid a false positive association. We demonstrate how to do this with simulated data. We calculate the posterior odds---a measurement of our relative belief for a common versus unrelated origin of a coincident NSBH and FRB. We find that a coincident <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>FRB</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>NSBH</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> from a common source can yield a statistically significant posterior odds in a network with at least two observatories, but only if we require a coincidence in time and sky location, rather than time alone. However, we find that, for our model, we require a network signal-to-noise ratio greater than 10 to be confident in the common-source detection, when using a threshold of ln odds <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>></mml:mo><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula>. We suggest that a coincident <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>NSBH</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>FRB</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> detection could help distinguish between FRB engines by discriminating between disrupting and nondisrupting models.

title: Fast Radio Bursts as Precursor Radio Emission from Monster Shocks
summary: It has been proposed recently that the breaking of magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) waves in the inner magnetosphere of strongly magnetized neutron stars can power different types of high-energy transients. Motivated by these considerations, we study the steepening and dissipation of a strongly magnetized fast magnetosonic wave propagating in a declining background magnetic field, by means of particle-in-cell simulations that encompass MHD scales. Our analysis confirms the formation of a monster shock as <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>E</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>--></mml:mo><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, that dissipates about half of the fast magnetosonic wave energy. It also reveals, for the first time, the generation of a high-frequency precursor wave by the monster shock, carrying a fraction of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula> of the total energy dissipated at the shock. The spectrum of the precursor wave exhibits several sharp harmonic peaks, with frequencies in the gigahertz band under conditions anticipated in magnetars. Such signals may appear as fast radio bursts.

title: Gravitational lensing of fast radio bursts: Prospects for probing microlens populations in lensing galaxies
summary: Gravitational lensing by a stellar microlens of mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> forms two images separated by microarcseconds on the sky and has a time delay of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> seconds. Although we cannot resolve such microimages in the sky, they could be resolved in time if the source is a fast radio burst (FRB). In this work, we study the magnification (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo></mml:math></inline-formula>) and time delay (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>) distributions of microimages led by different microlens populations. We find that, in microlensing of typical strongly lensed (macro)images in galaxy lenses, microimages stemmed from a population of stellar mass microlenses in the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>[</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.08</mml:mn><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn><mml:mo>]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> range and a second (dark) microlens population in <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>[</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>]</mml:mo><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> range reside in different parts of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mo>|</mml:mo><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>t</mml:mi><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> plane. For the global minimum macroimage, due to low stellar mass density, we find that the stellar population leads to peaks in autocorrelation at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>></mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula> seconds, whereas the secondary population leads to peaks at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula> seconds, allowing us to differentiate different microlens populations. However, an increase in stellar density introduces new peaks at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula> seconds, which can pollute the inference about the presence of multiple microlens populations. In addition, we also show that the number of microimages, hence the number of peaks in the autocorrelation, is sensitive to the underlying stellar mass function, allowing us to constrain the stellar initial mass function (IMF) with FRB microlesning in the future. This work is a first step toward using FRB lensing to probe the microlens population within strong lenses, and more detailed studies are required to assess the effect of various uncertainties that we only discussed qualitatively.

title: Phase transition and nuclear symmetry energy from neutron star observations: Constraints in light of PSR J0614-3329
summary: The possible occurrence of a first-order hadron-quark phase transition in neutron-star interiors remains an open question. Whether such a transition can be directly tested with improved observations is a key challenge. Here, we incorporate the latest constraints, especially a new radius measurement by the neutron star interior composition explorer for PSR J0614-3329, into a nonparametric Gaussian process equation of state framework that explicitly includes a first-order transition. We find a Bayes factor of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.3</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula> when comparing models with and without an explicit phase transition, marginally favoring its presence. At 68% credibility, the transition onset density <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>PT</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> is either below <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> (corresponding to masses <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>, with density jump <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>) or, more prominently, above <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> (near the central density of the heaviest neutron star, with <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>), where <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> represents the nuclear saturation density. In addition, by using symmetry-energy expansion at low densities (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.1</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>), we infer a slope parameter <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:msubsup><mml:mn>40.2</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>14.3</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>19.3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, in good agreement with nuclear-experiment values. Intriguingly, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>L</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> correlates positively with the radius difference between <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>2.0</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> stars.

title: Probability density function for dispersion measure of fast radio burst from extragalactic medium
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) have emerged as powerful probes in cosmology. An optimized method was recently proposed to extract the cosmic baryon density from localized FRBs by maximizing the joint likelihood function of the extragalactic dispersion measure (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>DM</mml:mi><mml:mi>ext</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>). In this paper, we identify a crucial factor that was omitted in the probability density function (PDF) for <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>DM</mml:mi><mml:mi>ext</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> in that method. Using simulated FRB data, we demonstrate that neglecting this factor leads to a systematic bias in the inferred cosmic baryon density, with deviations exceeding the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> confidence level. This highlights the necessity of including the missing factor for reliable cosmological applications of FRBs. Furthermore, applying our corrected PDF to a sample of 88 real localized FRBs, we find that the baryon density inferred with the original PDF is inconsistent with the Planck 2018 CMB results, whereas our corrected PDF yields excellent agreement.

title: Fastest spinning millisecond pulsars: Indicators for quark matter in neutron stars?
summary: We study rotating hybrid stars, with a particular emphasis on the effect of a deconfinement phase transition on their properties at high spin. Our analysis is based on a hybrid equation of state with a phase transition from hypernuclear matter to color-superconducting quark matter, where both phases are described within a relativistic density functional approach. By varying the vector meson and diquark couplings in the quark matter phase, we obtain different hybrid star sequences with varying extension of the quark matter core, ensuring consistency with astrophysical constraints from mass, radius, and tidal deformability measurements. As a result, we demonstrate the impact of an increasing rotational frequency on the maximum gravitational mass, the central energy density of compact stars, the appearance of the quasiradial oscillations, and nonaxisymmetric instabilities. We demonstrate that for the most favorable parameter sets with a strong vector coupling, hybrid star configurations with a color superconducting quark matter core can describe the fastest spinning and heaviest galactic neutron star PSR J0952-0607, while it is out of reach for the purely hadronic hypernuclear star configuration. We also revise the previously proposed empirical relation between the Kepler frequency, gravitational mass, and radius of nonrotating neutron stars, obtained based on the assumption that all neutron stars, up to the heaviest, are hadronic. We show how the phase transition to quark matter alters this relation and, consequently, the constraints on the dense matter equation of state. Our findings reveal that incorporating the hybrid equation of state has significant implications for the constraints on the properties of strongly interacting matter and neutron stars, placing the upper limit on <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo><=</mml:mo><mml:mn>14.90</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mn>0.7</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>11.49</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> (considering 716 Hz frequency limit from PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>1748</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>2446</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mi>ad</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>) and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo><=</mml:mo><mml:mn>11.90</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> (for 1000 Hz).

title: Bayesian analysis of the neutron star equation of state and model comparison: Insights from PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0437</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>4715</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0614</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>3329</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, and other multiphysics data
summary: We perform a comprehensive Bayesian analysis to constrain the neutron star (NS) equation of state (EoS) using a wide range of terrestrial and astrophysical data. The terrestrial inputs include quantities related to symmetric nuclear matter (SNM) and symmetry energy up to two times saturation density (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≃</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.16</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>fm</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>), derived from finite nuclei and heavy ion collisions (HIC). The astrophysical constraints incorporate NS radii and tidal deformabilities from recent Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) observations and GW170817, respectively. We consider five different EoS models: Taylor, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>n</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula>, Skyrme, relative mean field, and sound speed (CS), and analyze them by sequentially updating the priors with (i) chiral effective field theory (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi><mml:mi>EFT</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>)-based pure neutron matter, (ii) terrestrial, empirical, and earlier astrophysical data, (iii) case (ii) including NICER radii of PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0437</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>4715</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0614</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>3329</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, (iv) all data combined, and (v) excluding empirical nuclear inputs. We also perform Bayesian model comparison, which favors the Skyrme model under all combined data [scenario (iv)], yielding tight constraints on symmetry energy parameters: <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>L</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>56</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>sym</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>132</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>15</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, and also on SNM parameters: <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>K</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>265</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>12</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>Q</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>366</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>43</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>. The mass-radius and mass--tidal deformability posterior distributions are also well constrained. The radius and tidal deformability of a <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> neutron star are found to be <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>11.85</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.11</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>Λ</mml:mi><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>354</mml:mn><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>25</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula>, respectively.

title: Neutron stars with exceptionally light QCD axions
summary: We present a comprehensive study of axion condensed neutron stars that arise in models of an exceptionally light axion that couples to quantum chromodynamics (QCD). These axions solve the strong-charge-parity (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>) problem, but have a mass-squared lighter than that due to QCD by a factor of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula>. Inside dense matter, the axion potential is altered, and much of the matter in neutron stars resides in the axion condensed phase where the strong-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> parameter <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi>P</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> remains a good symmetry. In these regions, masses and interactions of nucleons are modified, in turn changing the equation of state (EOS), structure, and phenomenology of the neutron stars. We take the first steps toward the study of the EOS of neutron star matter at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> within chiral effective field theory and use relativistic mean field theory to deduce the resulting changes to nuclear matter and the neutron star low-density EOS. We derive constraints on the exceptionally light axion parameter space based on observations of the thermal relaxation of accreting neutron stars, isolated neutron star cooling, and pulsar glitches, excluding the region up to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>5</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>7</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mi>ϵ</mml:mi><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.2</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> for <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>9</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>. We comment on potential changes to the neutron star mass-radius relationship, and discuss the possibility of novel, nuclear-density compact objects with <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>θ</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mi>π</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> that are stabilized not by gravity but by the axion potential.

title: Induced Compton scattering in magnetized electron and positron pair plasma
summary: A formulation for the parametric instability of electromagnetic waves in magnetized pair plasma is developed. The linear growth rate of induced Compton scattering is derived analytically for frequencies below the cyclotron frequency for the first time. We identify three modes of density fluctuation: ordinary, charged, and neutral modes. In the charged mode, the ponderomotive force separates charges (electrons and positrons) longitudinally, in contrast to the nonmagnetized case. We also recognize two effects that significantly reduce the scattering rate for waves polarized perpendicular to the magnetic field: (1) the gyroradius effect due to the magnetic suppression of particle orbits and (2) Debye screening effect for wavelengths larger than the Debye length. Applying this to fast radio bursts, we find that these effects facilitate the escape of X-mode waves from the magnetosphere and outflow of a magnetar and neutron star, enabling 100% polarization as observed. Our formulation provides a foundation for consistently addressing the nonlinear interaction of electromagnetic waves with magnetized plasma in astrophysics and laser physics.

title: Polarization signals from axion-photon resonant conversion in a neutron star magnetosphere
summary: Neutron stars provide ideal astrophysical laboratories for probing new physics beyond the Standard Model. If axions exist, then photons can develop linear polarization during photon-axion conversion in the magnetic field of a neutron star. We find that the plasma in the neutron star magnetosphere could dramatically enhance the polarization through the resonant conversion effect. With the polarization measurements from PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mn>0656</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, 4U <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0142</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>61</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, and the benchmark polarization measurement in the midinfrared band, we demonstrate that optical and infrared polarization from neutron stars can provide strong constraints on the axion-photon coupling over a broad axion mass range <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>11</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>a</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>.

title: Assessing the impact of uniform rotation on the structure of neutron stars
summary: Driven by recent laboratory experiments and astronomical observations, significant advances have deepened our understanding of neutron-star physics. NICER's Pulse Profile Modeling has refined our knowledge of neutron star masses and radii, while gravitational-wave detections have revealed key insights into the structure of neutron stars. Particularly relevant is the extraction of the tidal deformability by the LIGO-Virgo collaboration and the most recent determination of stellar radii by NICER, both suggesting a relatively soft equation of state (EOS) at intermediate densities. Additionally, measurements from the PREX collaboration and from pulsar timing suggest instead that the EOS is stiff in the vicinity of saturation density and at the highest densities accessible to date. But how stiff can the EOS be at these very high densities? Recent events featuring compact objects near the ``lower mass gap'' have raised questions about the existence of very massive neutron stars. Motivated by this finding and in light of new refinements to theoretical models, we explore the possibility that these massive objects may indeed be rapidly rotating neutron stars. We explore how rotation affects both the maximum neutron star mass and their associated radii, and discuss the implications they may have on the equation of state.

title: Learning about neutron star composition from the slope of the mass-radius diagram
summary: The slope of the neutron star mass-radius curve, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, is studied to understand the information it may carry about the composition of neutron stars, particularly with regard to the presence of non-nucleonic degrees of freedom. This study uses two large sets of relativistic mean-field equations of state with either nucleonic or nucleonic and hyperonic degrees of freedom, and imposes constraints obtained from GW170817 and the pulsars PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0030</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0451</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0740</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>6620</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. It is shown that: (i) some mass-radius curves are characterized by a negative slope from one solar mass up to the maximum mass; (ii) other equations of state (EoSs) have a positive slope for a given range of masses below the maximum star mass. Within the set of models considered, the first set includes only a very small number of hyperonic EoSs: fewer than 0.5% of the total number of hyperonic stars and approximately one third of the nucleonic EoS. We have also analyzed the sign of the slope for neutron star masses of 1.2, 1.4 and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.8</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. Only approximately 1% of hyperonic EoSs predict a negative slope for <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> stars, whereas over 90% of nucleonic stars have a negative slope at this mass. Finally, almost all stars have a negative slope at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.8</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. A positive slope at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> may indicate the presence of non-nucleonic degrees of freedom within neutron stars. The nuclear matter property that distinguishes the different scenarios most clearly is the curvature of the symmetry energy. Nucleonic EoSs with a positive slope <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:mi>d</mml:mi><mml:mi>R</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> predict the highest values, which can exceed 100 MeV.

title: Rapidly spinning dark matter-admixed neutron stars
summary: Millisecond pulsars, representing the older neutron star population, are believed to have undergone a prolonged period of dark matter accumulation, resulting in a higher dark matter content. Their extreme rotation makes them unique laboratories for studying rapidly rotating neutron stars admixed with dark matter. In this work, we model uniformly rotating neutron stars with a dark matter component that rotates independently from the baryon matter, allowing for the investigation of both corotating and counterrotating scenarios. We examine the impact of dark matter rotation on the macroscopic properties of neutron stars, including the mass-radius relation, the mass-shedding Keplerian limit, and moments of inertia, for various dark matter particle masses and total fractions, considering both core and halo distributions. Our findings provide a more comprehensive understanding of how dark matter influences the equilibrium properties of rotating neutron stars, offering new insights into the astrophysical implications of self-interacting dark matter.

title: Structural response of neutron stars to rapid rotation and its impact on the braking index
summary: Pulsars are rotating neutron stars that are observed to be slowing down, implying a loss of their rotational energy. There can be several different physical mechanisms involved in their spin-down process. The properties of fast-rotating pulsars depend on the nature of the neutron star matter, which can also affect the spin-down mechanisms. In this work, we examine three different physical phenomena contributing to the spin-down: magnetic dipole radiation, gravitational mass quadrupole radiation due to the ``mountain'' formation, and gravitational mass current quadrupole radiation---or the r-modes---and calculate the expressions for the braking indices due to all of them. We have also considered the implications of the uncertainties of the equation of the state of neutron star matter and rapid rotation on the braking indices corresponding to the aforementioned processes and their combinations. In all cases, the rapid rotation results in a departure of the braking index from the standard values when the rotational effects are ignored. If generated with a saturation amplitude within the range of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, the r-mode oscillations dominate the spin-down of millisecond pulsars. Moreover, we explore the braking index in the context of millisecond magnetars. We also study the effects of different choices of baryon mass on the braking indices.

title: Origin of nucleon mass in the light of PSR J0614-3329 with quark-hadron crossover
summary: The recent NICER observation of PSR J0614-3329, revealing the smallest reliably measured neutron star radius of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>R</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>10.2</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mn>9</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.86</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.01</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> at mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>=</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msubsup><mml:mn>4</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.07</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.06</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msubsup><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>, provides an unprecedented constraint on the equation of state of dense matter. We investigate the implications of this measurement for the origin of nucleon mass within the parity doublet model framework, which naturally incorporates both chiral variant and chiral invariant mass components. We construct unified equations of state by employing the parity doublet model with isovector scalar meson <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>a</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>(</mml:mo><mml:mn>980</mml:mn><mml:mo>)</mml:mo></mml:math></inline-formula> for hadronic matter up to twice nuclear saturation density, smoothly connected to a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio-type quark model at higher densities through a crossover transition. By systematically varying the chiral invariant mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> and quark matter parameters, we determine which values simultaneously satisfy all current astrophysical constraints, including gravitational wave observations from GW170817, NICER measurements of several pulsars, and the existence of two-solar-mass neutron stars. The inclusion of PSR J0614-3329 dramatically refines the allowed range of the chiral invariant mass from the previous constraint of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>580</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mn>860</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>800</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mn>860</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>MeV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, raising the lower bound by approximately 220 MeV. This result indicates that the chiral invariant mass must constitute at least 85% of the nucleon mass, challenging the traditional picture of nucleon mass generation through spontaneous chiral symmetry breaking alone and highlighting the importance of gluon condensation and other nonchiral mechanisms.

title: Testing scalar dark matter clumps with pulsar timing arrays
summary: Scalar dark matter is a viable alternative to particle dark matter models such as weakly interacting massive particles. This is particularly the case for scalars with a low mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>21</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> as required to make quantum effects macroscopic on galactic scales. We point out that by synchronizing the measurements of arrival times of pairs of pulsars, pulsar timing arrays could probe ultralight dark matter (ULDM) scenarios with a mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>23</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>19</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> that is greater than the one reached in standard analysis. The upper limit on the mass <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> is set by the time lag <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> between the observations of the two pulsars and could be pushed above <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>19</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>eV</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> for <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> smaller than one hour. However, for these high scalar masses only very high density dark matter clouds could be detected and the capture rate of neutron stars is too low to provide sufficient statistics. Significant detection probabilities would thus require direct dark-matter-baryon interactions that favor the formation of neutron stars within such dark matter clouds, or the discovery of black hole/pulsar binary systems, taking advantage of the dark matter spike generated by the black hole.

title: Relativistic mean-field predictions for the dense-matter equation of state and application to neutron stars
summary: Relativistic mean-field models (RMF) based on the exchange of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>ω</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> mesons including nonlinear nucleon-<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>σ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> couplings and density-dependent <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>ρ</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> coupling, are considered. A large set of models is generated using the Markov chain Monte Carlo approach and Bayesian statistics to reproduce nuclear physics knowledge encoded in terms of the nuclear empirical parameters and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi><mml:mi>EFT</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> predictions for low-density neutron matter. These models are filtered, in a second step, using astrophysical constraints: the tidal deformability obtained from GW170817 parameter estimation and the observational masses deduced from radioastronomy. We then obtain a set of selected RMF models that are compatible with present nuclear and astrophysical constraints and that can be employed to make predictions and to quantity their uncertainties. Predictions for masses and radii are compared to NICER masses-radii analyses for PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0030</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0451</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0740</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>6620</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. We find that RMF models can be made soft enough to predict low values for neutron star radii compatible with GW170817 and, at larger densities, stiff enough to be compatible with NICER analyses for massive neutron stars. Our models can also reach large values for the maximum mass, up to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>2.6</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. In addition, for the core composition, we obtain a large distribution of the proton fraction for canonical mass neutron stars, some of them allowing the direct URCA fast cooling process. For massive neutron stars, however, most of our models suggest a large proton fraction in the core allowing direct URCA fast cooling process.

title: Exploring fermionic dark matter admixed neutron stars in the light of astrophysical observations
summary: We studied the properties of dark matter admixed-neutron stars (DMANS), considering fermionic dark matter (DM) that interacts gravitationally with hadronic matter (HM). Using relativistic mean-field equations of state (EOSs) for both components, we solved the two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations to determine neutron star (NS) properties assuming that DM is confined within the stellar core. For hadronic matter, we employed realistic EOSs derived from low energy nuclear physics experiments, heavy-ion collision data, and NS observations. To constrain key dark matter parameters---such as particle mass, mass fraction, and the coupling to mass ratio---we applied Bayesian inference, incorporating various astrophysical data including mass, radii, and NICER mass-radius distributions for PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0740</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>6620</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0030</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0451</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. Additionally, we explored the influence of high-density HM EOSs and examined the impact of stiffer hadronic EOSs, excluding the vector meson self-interaction term. Our findings indicate that current astrophysical observations primarily constrain the dark matter fraction, while providing limited constraints on the particle mass or coupling. However, the dark matter fraction is largely insensitive to how astrophysical observations or uncertainties in the high-density EOS are incorporated. Instead, it is predominantly determined by the stiffness of the hadronic EOS at high densities, with stiffer hadronic EOSs yielding a higher dark matter mass fraction. Therefore, we conclude that the dark matter fraction plays a crucial role in shaping the properties of DMANS. Future investigations incorporating more realistic EOSs and astrophysical observations of other compact objects may provide deeper insights into dark matter.

title: Systematics from NICER pulse profiles drive uncertainty in multimessenger inference of the neutron star equation of state
summary: We present new constraints on the neutron star equation of state (EOS) and mass distribution using a unified Bayesian inference framework that incorporates the latest NICER measurements, including PSR J0614-3329, alongside gravitational-wave data, radio pulsar masses, and nuclear theory. By systematically comparing four inference scenarios---varying in the inclusion of PSR J0614-3329 and in the pulse profile model used for PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0030</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0451</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>---we quantify the impact of observational and modeling choices on dense matter inference. We find that systematics from hotspot geometry dominate EOS uncertainties: the choice of hotspot geometry for PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0030</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0451</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> leads to significant shifts in the inferred stiffness of the EOS and maximum neutron star mass. In contrast, PSR J0614-3329 mildly softens the EOS at low densities, reducing the radius at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.4</mml:mn><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> by <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>. A Bayesian model comparison yields a Bayes factor of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>log</mml:mi><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:msub><mml:mi>BF</mml:mi><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.58</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula> in favor of the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>ST</mml:mi><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mi>PDT</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> hotspot model over PDT-U, providing strong evidence that multimessenger EOS inference can statistically discriminate between competing NICER pulse profile models. These results highlight the critical role of NICER systematics in dense matter inference and the power of joint analyses in breaking modeling degeneracies.

title: Long-term impact of the magnetic-field strength on the evolution and electromagnetic emission by neutron-star merger remnants
summary: Numerical simulations are essential to understand the complex physics accompanying the merger of binary systems of neutron stars. However, these simulations become computationally challenging when they have to model the merger remnants on timescales over which secular phenomena, such as the launching of magnetically driven outflows, develop. To tackle these challenges, we have recently developed a hybrid approach that combines, via a handoff transition, a fully general-relativistic code (FIL) with a more efficient code making use of the conformally flat approximation (BHAC+). We report here important additional developments of BHAC+ consisting of the inclusion of gravitational-wave radiation-reaction contributions and of higher-order formulations of the equations of general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamics. Both improvements have allowed us to explore binary neutron-star merger remnants with high accuracy and over timescales that would have been computationally prohibitive otherwise. More specifically, we have investigated the impact of the magnetic-field strength on the long-term (i.e., <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>200</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>ms</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>) and high-resolution (i.e., 150 m) evolutions of the ``magnetar'' resulting from the merger of two neutron stars with a realistic equation of state. In this way, and for sufficiently large magnetic fields, we observe the weakening or suppression of differential rotation and the generation of magnetic flares in the outer layers of the remnant. These flares, driven mostly by the Parker instability, are responsible for intense and collimated Poynting flux outbursts and mass ejections. This novel phenomenology offers the possibility of seeking corresponding signatures from the observations of short gamma-ray bursts and hence revealing the existence of a long-lived strongly magnetized remnant.

title: Reexamining constraints on neutron star properties from perturbative QCD
summary: The implications of perturbative QCD (pQCD) calculations on neutron stars are carefully examined. While pQCD calculations above baryon chemical potentials <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.4</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> GeV demonstrate the potential of ruling out a wide range of neutron star equations of state (EOSs), such constraints only affect the most massive neutron stars in the vicinity of the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff limit, resulting in constraints that are orthogonal to current or expected astrophysical bounds. In the most constraining scenario, pQCD considerations favor low values of the squared speed sound <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> at high <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> relevant for the most massive neutron stars, but leave predictions of the radii and tidal deformabilities almost unchanged. Such considerations become irrelevant if the maximum speed of sound squared inside neutron stars does not exceed about <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>C</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>max</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, or if pQCD breaks down below <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.9</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> GeV. Furthermore, the large pQCD uncertainties preclude any meaningful bounds on the neutron star EOS at the moment. Interestingly, if pQCD predictions for the pressure at around <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> GeV are refined and found to be low (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>≲</mml:mo><mml:mn>1.5</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> GeV/<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>fm</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mn>3</mml:mn></mml:msup></mml:math></inline-formula>), evidence for a soft neutron star inner core EOS in combination with the existence of two-solar-mass pulsars would indicate the presence of color superconductivity beyond neutron star densities. I point out that two-solar-mass pulsars place robust upper bounds on this nonperturbative effect and require the pairing gap to be less than <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>∆</mml:mi><mml:mi>CFL</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo><=</mml:mo><mml:mn>500</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mtext>MeV</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> at <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>μ</mml:mi><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>≈</mml:mo><mml:mn>2.5</mml:mn><mml:mspace></mml:mspace><mml:mtext>GeV</mml:mtext></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>.

title: Axionlike particle mediated dark matter and neutron star properties in the quantum hadrodynamics model
summary: We investigate the effects of the axionlike particle (ALP)-mediated dark matter (DM) model on neutron star properties using the quantum hadrodynamics model (QHD). Using the relativistic mean-field approximation with the QHD-ALP-DM framework, we compute the equation of state (EoS) of neutron stars. Based on our previous study, we find that typical ALP parameter values have no significant effect on the EoS. We then explore various parametrizations of this model by varying the DM Fermi momentum, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>, and DM mass, <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. Our results show that increasing <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>q</mml:mi><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> or <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>m</mml:mi><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> shifts the energy density to higher values while reducing the maximum mass, radius, and tidal deformability of neutron stars. Finally, comparison with observational constraints from gravitational wave events and pulsar measurements indicates that the allowed parameter space for this model is constrained to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>q</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>f</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.05</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>GeV</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>m</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>1000</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>GeV</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. As a result, our study highlights the importance of next-generation gamma-ray observatories, such as the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), in probing the ALP-mediated DM model.

title: Breaking the baryon density-Hubble constant degeneracy in fast radio burst applications with associated gravitational waves
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are a unique probe of the cosmos, owing to dispersion caused by free electrons in the intergalactic medium. Two of the main quantities of interest are degenerate: the density of matter <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> outside of galaxies and the Hubble constant <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. Here, we present a new possibility of breaking the degeneracy without invoking early-Universe priors on <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula>. Assuming some FRBs originate in compact object mergers, the combination of dispersion and luminosity distance from the gravitational wave (GW) can be used to measure <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> (where <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>h</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> is the dimensionless Hubble constant). We show that this measurement can be combined with the abundant FRBs that have a redshift measurement. This combination breaks the degeneracy with the Hubble constant. We develop a Bayesian framework and forecast that third-generation GW detectors are required to obtain meaningful constraints. We forecast that 1 year of Einstein Telescope operations can constrain <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>H</mml:mi><mml:mn>0</mml:mn></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>±</mml:mo><mml:mn>6</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>Mpc</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ω</mml:mi><mml:mi>b</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:msup><mml:mi>h</mml:mi><mml:mn>2</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:msub><mml:mi>f</mml:mi><mml:mi>d</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> to <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mfrac><mml:mrow><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0015</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>0.0016</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:mfrac></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> (68% credible interval). The method can also be used with luminosity distances obtained through other means than GWs.

title: Slowly rotating neutron stars in aether scalar-tensor theory
summary: Aether scalar-tensor theory is a relativistic alternative gravity model that behaves like cold dark matter on cosmological scales while predicting the MOND force-law in astrophysical systems. The theory correctly predicts the cosmic microwave background and linear matter power spectra, and the mass discrepancies observed across the Universe. We derive and solve the equations governing neutron stars in aether scalar tensor theory at first-order in slow rotation, finding that the theory predicts approximate universal relations between the moment of inertia and the compactness (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>I</mml:mi><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:mi>C</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> relations) that differ from their general relativity counterparts. These relations may enable tests of aether scalar-tensor theory using x-ray observations of pulsars and gravitational wave observations of binary neutron star mergers.

title: Impact of dark matter distribution on neutron star properties
summary: We investigate the structural and observable impacts of dark matter (DM) on neutron stars (NSs) using a combined equation of state that integrates the relativistic mean-field (RMF) model for baryonic matter with a variable density profile for DM, incorporating DM-baryon interactions mediated by the Higgs field. Employing three RMF parameter sets (NL3, BigApple, and IOPB-I) for baryonic matter, we analyze mass-radius relations, maximum mass, and tidal deformability, focusing on DM density scaling (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>) and steepness (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>) parameters. Our findings reveal that increased DM concentration significantly enhances NS compactness, shifting mass-radius profiles and reducing tidal deformability. The DM influence strongly depends on the steepness of the DM density profile, where high <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> values lead to strongly confined DM within the NS core, resulting in more compact and less deformable configurations. Observational constraints from PSR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0740</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>6620</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and GW170817 impose consistent structural limits on DM fractions across different equations of state models, narrowing the allowable parameter space for DM and linking specific combinations of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>α</mml:mi><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> (<inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mi>χ</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> being the mass of dark matter particle) and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> values to viable NS structures. This study highlights the interplay among DM concentration, nuclear stiffness, and observational data in shaping NS structure, offering insights into future constraints on DM in high-density astrophysical environments.

title: Scalarized neutron stars with a highly relativistic core in scalar-tensor gravity
summary: Compact stars in scalar-tensor (ST) gravity have been extensively investigated, but relatively few studies have focused on highly relativistic neutron stars (NSs) with an extremely dense core region where the trace of the energy-momentum tensor reverses its sign. In this regime, we identify the origin of the phenomenon where multiple scalarized solutions exist for a fixed central density, arising from the oscillatory profile of the scalar field inside the star. This origin further indicates that the multibranch structure emerges for both negative and positive <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula>, the quadratic-term coefficient in the effective coupling function between the scalar field and conventional matter in the Einstein frame. By comparing the Damour--Esposito-Farèse and Mendes-Ortiz models of the ST gravity, we demonstrate that their distinct scalarization behaviors stem from whether the effective coupling function is bounded. We also compute for scalarized NSs with a highly relativistic dense core in ST theories the moment of inertia and tidal deformability that are relevant to pulsar-timing and gravitational-wave experiments.

title: Minimum Neutron Star Mass in Neutrino-Driven Supernova Explosions
summary: Supernova theory has struggled to explain the lightest known neutron star candidate with an accurate mass determination, the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1.174</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>M</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> companion in the eccentric compact binary system <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mi>J</mml:mi><mml:mn>0453</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>1559</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. To improve the theoretical lower limit for neutron star birth masses, we perform 3D supernova simulations for five stellar models close to the minimum mass for iron core collapse. We obtain a record-low neutron star mass of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.192</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and a substantial kick of <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>100</mml:mn><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>km</mml:mi><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mi>s</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>-</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. Given residual uncertainties in stellar evolution, a neutron star origin for the <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mn>1.174</mml:mn><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>M</mml:mi><mml:mo>⊙</mml:mo></mml:msub></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> object remains plausible.

title: Toward a unified hadron-quark equation of state for neutron stars within the relativistic mean-field model
summary: The equation of state of dense matter remains a central challenge in astrophysics and high-energy physics, particularly at supranuclear densities where exotic degrees of freedom like hyperons or deconfined quarks are expected to appear. Neutron stars provide a unique natural laboratory to probe this regime. In this work, we present EVA--01, a novel equation of state that provides a unified description of dense matter by incorporating both hadron and quark degrees of freedom within a single relativistic mean-field Lagrangian, from which the equation of state is derived at finite temperature. The model extends the density-dependent formalism by introducing a Polyakov-loop-inspired scalar field to dynamically govern the hadron-quark phase transition, following the approach of chiral mean-field models. The resulting model is consistent with a wide range of theoretical and observational constraints, including those from chiral effective field theory, massive pulsars, gravitational-wave events, and NICER data. We analyze its thermodynamic properties by constructing the QCD phase diagram, identifying the deconfinement, chiral, and nuclear liquid-gas transitions. As a first application, we model the evolution of protoneutron stars using isentropic snapshots and explore the implications of the slow stable hybrid star hypothesis. Our findings establish EVA--01 as a robust and versatile framework for exploring dense matter, bridging the gap between microphysical models and multimessenger astrophysical observations.

title: Revealing the internal magnetic fields of magnetars via their associated periodic signals
summary: The magnetic deformation of magnetars is affected by their internal magnetic fields, which are generally difficult to be measured directly through observations. In this work, the periodic pulse-phase modulations in the hard x-ray emissions of the magnetars 4U <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>0142</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>61</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, 1E 1547.0-5408, SGR <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1900</mml:mn><mml:mo>+</mml:mo><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>, and SGR 1806-20, and the periodicities of fast radio bursts (FRBs) 180916 and 121102 are interpreted as free precession of the (host) magnetars. Using these periodic signals, we investigate the magnetars' internal magnetic fields. In order to simultaneously account for the modulation periods and surface thermal emissions of the former four magnetars, and require that their internal poloidal fields smoothly connect with the surface dipole fields, the parameter that characterizes the distribution of toroidal field in the magnetar interior should satisfy <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mi>β</mml:mi><mml:mo>≳</mml:mo><mml:mn>1</mml:mn></mml:math></inline-formula>. Moreover, their volume-averaged strengths of poloidal and toroidal fields are respectively <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mover><mml:mrow><mml:mi>B</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mo>̄</mml:mo></mml:mrow></mml:mover></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>14</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>15</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mover><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>̄</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mn>10</mml:mn><mml:mn>15</mml:mn></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>G</mml:mi></mml:math></inline-formula> with the strength ratios <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:msub><mml:mover><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>̄</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>t</mml:mi></mml:msub><mml:mo>/</mml:mo><mml:msub><mml:mover><mml:mi>B</mml:mi><mml:mo>̄</mml:mo></mml:mover><mml:mi>p</mml:mi></mml:msub></mml:math></inline-formula> generally distributing within <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:mo>~</mml:mo><mml:mn>2</mml:mn><mml:mi>--</mml:mi><mml:mn>37</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>. We could also constrain the critical temperature for neutron superfluidity in the neutron-star core considering that the former four magnetars are probably precessing, and the most stringent constraint is <inline-formula><mml:math><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mrow><mml:mi>T</mml:mi></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mi>c</mml:mi><mml:mo>,</mml:mo><mml:mi>core</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:mo><</mml:mo><mml:mn>6.4</mml:mn><mml:mo>×</mml:mo><mml:msup><mml:mrow><mml:mn>10</mml:mn></mml:mrow><mml:mrow><mml:mn>8</mml:mn></mml:mrow></mml:msup><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mtext> </mml:mtext><mml:mi>K</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:math></inline-formula>.
